- green: TDD Green Phase

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

Rule 1 satisfied: 13 passing.

**Naming Evaluation (first priority)**

- `basePremiumOfGroup` — takes a same-type group; the block rule only applies to component groups. Name is accurate but the "group" concept is under-specified. Acceptable.
- `groupByType` — accurate.
- `COMPONENT_TYPES` / `isComponent` — accurate, reveals the component-only nature of the block rule.
- `quotePremium`, `totalBasePremium`, `roundPremium` — all accurate.
- `BLOCK_SIZE` / `BLOCK_BASE_PREMIUM` — accurate.

No renames needed; naming already reveals intent.

**APP mass — `groupByType` (the heaviest element)**

```
const groups = new Map(...)          bindings 1 + invocation 2       = 3
for (const item of items)            loop 5 + binding 1 + binding 1  = 7
const group = groups.get(...) ?? []  binding 1 + inv 2 + cond 4 + const 1 = 8
group.push(item)                     invocation 2                    = 2
groups.set(item.type, group)         invocation 2                    = 2
return [...groups.values()]          invocation 2                    = 2
```
Total mass: **24**, and it uses a mutable accumulator (`push`/`set`) — assignments-by-mutation, the highest-mass category in APP.

**Refactoring applied**: replaced the imperative grouping loop with `Map.groupBy`-style reduction expressed declaratively.

content.text:
All 13 tests still green.

## Refactor Phase Complete

**Naming evaluation (first priority)**: no renames needed. `basePremiumOfGroup`, `totalBasePremium`, `quotePremium`, `roundPremium`, `BLOCK_SIZE`, `BLOCK_BASE_PREMIUM`, `COMPONENT_TYPES`, and `isComponent` all already describe what they do given the 13 tests. The Green phase's `isComponent` in particular correctly encodes that the block is a component-only rule, matching the "3 swords → 335" test.

**Refactoring applied**: rewrote `groupByType` in `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-09-05_11-06-59_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.1.5-pure-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking-4/src/claim-office.ts`. It was the only imperative element left in an otherwise declarative module — a `for` loop building a `Map` via `push`/`set`.

```ts
const distinctTypes = (items: Item[]): string[] => [...new Set(items.map((item) => item.type))];

const groupByType = (items: Item[]): Item[][] =>
  distinctTypes(items).map((type) => items.filter((item) => item.type === type));
```

**APP mass**: 24 → 16 (Δ −8). The loop (5) and the `?? []` conditional (4) are gone, as are the two mutating invocations; the cost added back is the `map`/`filter` iteration and the extra `distinctTypes` invocation.

I went through an intermediate version first — a `reduce` with `groups.set(...)` as the accumulator — and rejected it despite a similar mass score. It relied on `Map.set`'s return value to thread the accumulator, which the reader has to decode, and rebuilt the array on every item. Rule 2 trumps APP, so I took the `distinctTypes` + `filter` form instead: it reads as the literal statement of what a type-grouping is, and the extracted `distinctTypes` names a concept the block rule depends on. Worth noting the `filter` version is O(types × items) rather than O(items); at kata scale that is irrelevant, but if a later test introduces large item lists it is the reason to revisit.

**Not changed, with reasoning**: no duplication exists to extract (Rule 3) — the surcharge and fee arithmetic each appear once. Rule 4 is satisfied; I considered inlining `isComponent` into `basePremiumOfGroup` as one fewer element, but the named predicate is what makes the component-only nature of the block rule legible, so the element earns its place. `runStep`'s `throw` for the unsupported `claim` op is correct as a not-yet-implemented marker — several `it.todo` claim tests will drive that out.
